s07.slug: THURSDAY · 8:00 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT — THE ODYSSEY
body: The sodium lamps over the Anacapa lot turn everything the same burnt orange: the peeling eucalyptus along the far edge, the parking stripes, the bike cage, and Kevin’s mother’s Honda Odyssey, whatever color it is by day. It is backed into its space under the window of 420 with the hatch up and the dome light on. The La Vang rosary hangs from the mirror. The TRAN first-aid kit is strapped to the back of the passenger seat with two bungee cords, one more than it has ever needed. The cooler waits on the asphalt behind the bumper. Out of the open hatch, at a volume a mother would sign off on, comes the first of the two Carpenters songs on Kevin’s *Road Trip Mix*.

Kevin is at the driver’s door in his quarter-zip, holding a clipboard against his chest like a chart at a bedside. Taped to the dash at all four corners is a seating chart Jack can’t read from the back of the van. Beside it, taped the same way, is a new index card in Kevin’s block capitals.

body.title: Taped to the dash, beside the chart
body.text: SPEED: 65. NOT 66. · OIL AT THE AZ LINE. · GAS AT HALF A TANK, NOT A QUARTER. · RECEIPTS TO LENA.

body: Somewhere on Glenwood Avenue, Frank Costigan has been beaten to the oil by a pre-med.

Kevin has a second sheet, folded in quarters. He leans across the passenger seat, puts it in the glovebox and goes back to his clipboard, and Theo, passing the open door with his weekender, gives the glovebox two pats until it clicks shut, and keeps walking.

body.text: Jack has come up from Del Playa by way of 412 at something close to a jog, with the duffel over his shoulder and Gloria’s pie in both hands, level. Laney is at the back of the van sorting a row of canvas totes along the bumper, each one labeled in black tape. She peels off the one marked FIREMAN, LARGE and holds it out to him without looking at him. “You missed the unveiling.”
body.else: Jack has come down the stairs behind Theo with the duffel on one shoulder and FIREMAN, LARGE on the other, the label tape already lifting at one corner, and Gloria’s pie in both hands, level. Laney is at the back of the van sorting a row of canvas totes along the bumper. She sees her bag on him and goes on sorting.

body: Clare Dominguez is here in her 49ers cap, with a steel thermos she gives to Kevin as soon as he has a hand free. While he is still holding it she leans in past him and wedges a holy card into the driver’s visor: Our Lady of La Vang in a gold áo dài, the Child on her arm. “For the roads,” Clare says. “It’s coffee in there. It’s strong. Don’t let Theo have any.”
“Slander,” says Theo, from inside the van.

At five past eight the side door of Delgado lets Lena out. Jack has the cooler by both handles, halfway up to the bumper, and what he gets of her is what comes in at the edge of things: one bag on a shoulder, a cardboard box riding a hip, boots on the asphalt. He doesn’t raise his head. She doesn’t look over. She sets the box down by the back tire and speaks to Kevin, at Jack’s elbow.
“Kevin, the cooler goes in last.”
Kevin, to Jack, who is holding the cooler: “The cooler goes in last.”
“I heard,” Jack says, to Kevin.
“He heard,” Kevin says, to the parking lot.

Jack puts the cooler back down where it was. Lena takes a yellow legal pad out of her bag and uncaps a pen. It is a parking lot and a van, and she is somebody with an opinion about a cooler, and he has a duffel that needs a place to go, and at that size it suits him fine.

It runs that way from there. The bench in the way-back folds forward, Lena tells Kevin, and the soft bags go under it. Kevin says so to Jack. Jack wants to know whether a duffel counts as soft, and asks Kevin, and Kevin turns around and asks the hatch, where Lena is writing on the pad, and the answer comes back by the same route, Lena to Kevin to Jack, with the small delay of a call from the space station. Duffels are soft.

“I’m pre-med,” Kevin says, setting the second of Laney’s three suitcases in on its side. “I’m not a switchboard.” He looks at the third, still waiting on the asphalt. “Three suitcases for ten days is a presentation, Laney. I’d want to run tests.”
“Laney.” Lena’s pen keeps moving. “Would you let him know the bench is a seat. Bags go under it, not on it. People are going to sit there for thirty hours.”
“I am not *Western Union*, Lena.”

Laney turns around anyway and delivers it to Jack, every word, in a voice like a frost advisory for the higher elevations. “The bench is a seat. Bags go under it. Not on it. People are going to sit there for thirty hours.”
Jack takes his duffel off the bench and puts it on the asphalt.
“And that’s the last free one,” Laney says, to everybody. “Anybody else needs a thing said, I charge by the syllable, and y’all know I’m not cheap.”
Theo puts his head out of the side door. “Kevin, tell Lena that if we’re assigning the floor —”
“No,” Kevin says.

The head withdraws. A minute later Theo tries the lot at large, one hand up to frame it. “Picture it. Six friends. One minivan. Nineteen hundred miles of open road, and at the end of it a city that has waited forty-three years for —” Not one of them looks up. He lets the rest of the sentence walk off across the asphalt by itself and gets very busy with Margot’s milk crate.

Margot is sitting sideways in the open side door with her Docs on the running board and the crate at her feet: Interstate 10 printed out county by county in three colors of highlighter, and a Radio Shack tape recorder with its red light on. “Field season,” she says, when Jack looks at the light. “I closed the archive last night. Seven versions. In the seventh the dog gives an interview.”

Four floors up, the window of 420 scrapes open, and Doug Pruitt leans out of it in silhouette with something between his fingers that glows when he breathes in. “COSTIGAN.” He waits for the lot to look up, and the lot does. “IS THE DOG GOING?”
“Nobody answer him,” Kevin says.

The lot goes on loading. Laney reorganizes a tote she has already organized. Theo reads the label on the first-aid kit. Margot’s red light takes it all down, and after a while the window scrapes shut.

Kevin comes past with the third of Laney’s suitcases, beaming at both ends of the van. “Fun fact,” he says. “I’m going to spend my life telling people things they don’t want to hear, in rooms they can’t leave. I really thought I’d get to start in a hospital.” The smile holds. He puts the suitcase in.
When Jack brings his money over, Kevin has the treasurer’s binder clip out and doesn’t reach for it. “Your share’s paid.”
“By who?”
Kevin looks at Theo. Theo is reading the first-aid kit again.

Jack takes out Gloria’s envelope, COSTIGAN across the front in grease pencil, and counts it into Kevin’s palm under the dome light, in the Anchor’s ones and fives, gone soft in the share jar: fives up to fifty-five, then ones, and the sixty-first is a single with somebody’s phone number on it in ballpoint. Kevin regards the money in his hand. He pulls three twenties and a one out of the binder clip and holds them out sideways, and Theo takes his own money back and puts it inside his blazer without a word.
At the hatch Lena writes something on the pad. She doesn’t look up.
At twenty past eight Clare has a rehearsal. She tugs the brim of the cap at the van in general and says to Kevin, “Call me from Texas.”
“I will.”

She heads off across the lot toward the music building with her hands in her peacoat. Kevin watches her as far as the bike cage with his big easy smile on, the one that never quite reaches his eyes, and then he looks down at the clipboard and turns a page.
The pie comes next. “It can’t ride in cargo,” Kevin says. “Not on the floor.”
“Kevin, sugar, if you say *cargo* one more time tonight I will load you,” Laney says. “Not on the floor.”
“A pie on a floor mat,” Theo says. “Gila Bend. They find the box in the morning. It’s a horror picture.”
Margot holds out both arms. “Give it to me. For science.”

Jack gives it to her. She settles it across her knees in the side door with Gloria’s five, ringed in grease pencil, faced up into the dome light, and lays both hands on the lid. “It sleeps in 305,” she says. “I’ll be up.”

At the hatch Laney and Theo pass each other, an armload each, and on the way by a folded yellow sheet goes from his hand into hers. Laney puts it in her bra. Theo looks up at the stars, of which the Anacapa lot has three, one of them a plane.

Margot hasn’t taken her hands off the pie. “In some societies,” she says, “a man may not speak to his mother-in-law. Everything goes through a third party. Radcliffe-Brown called it an *avoidance relationship*. He thought it kept the peace between people with a dangerous amount in common.”
“Margot,” says Laney. “*Hush.*”
Theo reaches into the front and turns the Carpenters up a notch. No one stops him.
That leaves the seats. Kevin lifts the clipboard to start on them, and two people speak to him at once from opposite ends of the van.
“Kevin, I’ll take the way-back,” Lena says.
“Kevin, I’ll take the way-back,” Jack says.
Kevin closes his eyes. “There’s one way-back.”
“It seats three,” says Margot.
“No it does *not*,” says Laney.

body.text: Theo finds something urgent to do with the zipper on his weekender.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research. Took Skye’s side about the rose. Goffman, 1956. Wrote TED in her notebook and underlined it. Gave to Partners In Health and sent the rest of us there — Farmer’s Catholic, sort of. Commented ‘Front stage.’ on my status. Wednesday night in the lounge, while Laney kept it short with Theo: keeping score. A page in her notebook says SKYE. Thursday at the Anchor she interviewed Skye for her column. She hated that it was good. Her column ran Thursday: ‘Front Stage.’ It’s good. I told her twice. Thursday she brought Salinger’s death to the window table like a lab result. Friday in the Fishbowl she took Skye on about the fundraiser: a room raised for a cause, handed to its opposition. Skye said she didn’t hand them the room, she introduced them to me, and she’s still voting for Boxer. Margot gave her one point and kept one. Four versions of Wednesday are going around Delgado, she says. Commented *Back region. Finally.* on the taco picture. Monday night in the Fishbowl: six versions of Wednesday now. One has reached the Classics department. She wouldn’t read me any of them. Thursday night at the van she took the pie on her lap, for science, and named the rule: an avoidance relationship. Radcliffe-Brown. A man who may not speak to his mother-in-law; everything through a third party.

journal.title: Clare Dominguez
journal.text: Clare Dominguez. Newman sophomore. Plays violin in the Mass band. Played ‘Ashokan Farewell’ at the Haiti table and people stopped on the lawn. Kevin’s mother knows her mother. Everybody’s mother knows her mother. Four brothers, back in San Jose. Knows football better than Kevin. Wore a 49ers cap to Sully’s. At the Walk for Life a man with a megaphone screamed at her, and she kept praying. Skye stood in front of her. Thursday at eight she came to the lot with a thermos for Kevin and a holy card of Our Lady of La Vang. Call me from Texas. She left at twenty past.

response: Kevin opens his eyes. “God bless you,” he says, with feeling, and leans through the open door and taps the chart on the dash. “Middle captain’s chair, right side. Your back to the way-back. Which is where I put you in the first place.”

He runs his finger down it so everyone can see: Kevin at the wheel; Theo riding shotgun, labeled THE PRODUCER; Margot middle left; Jack middle right; and in the way-back, Laney on the right and Lena on the left, behind Margot. “It’s been final since before anybody asked me,” Kevin says, and pulls his head back out of the van.

choices.text: “Tell her I called the way-back in 2009.”
response: Kevin looks at Laney. Laney sighs from the bottom of her boots and relays it to the hatch word for word, flat as a weather map. “He called the way-back in 2009.”
Lena, to Laney, with the pen still going: “Tell him it’s 2010.”
Laney turns back to Jack. “It’s 2010.”

“Thank you both,” Kevin says. He holds the clipboard up at arm’s length like an eye chart, and on it is the same chart that’s taped to the dash, drawn before anybody asked him: Kevin at the wheel; Theo riding shotgun, labeled THE PRODUCER; Margot middle left; Jack middle right; Laney and Lena in the way-back, Lena on the left, behind Margot. “Read me the bottom line,” Kevin says. From where Jack stands it reads fine.

choices.text: “Put me as far from the way-back as the car goes.”
response: Kevin, very quietly: “That’s the hood.”
At the hatch a strap is pulled tight, hard, the buckle ratcheting. Jack doesn’t turn.

Kevin doesn’t lift the clipboard. He just points, one seat at a time, the chart he drew in the first place: himself at the wheel; Theo up front; Margot middle left; Jack middle right, his back to the way-back; and in the way-back, Laney, and on the left, behind Margot, Lena. He keeps the finger up until everyone has seen where it went.

s07a.slug: THURSDAY · 8:40 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT — THE BOX FROM OAKLAND
body: The box is the last thing left on the asphalt. Somebody packed it with care: brown paper over the cardboard, the corners folded hospital-tight, twine both ways and knotted on top, and across the lid in a careful upright hand, FOR MRS. BROUSSARD. In the corner, smaller, a return address: J. PARK-ELLIS, and a street in Oakland.
“Where does Julian go?” Kevin says.
“On top of the cooler,” says Margot, from behind the pie.

Kevin sets it on top of the cooler at the hatch end, lined up with the edges, and steps back from it. Margot’s recorder clicks off at the end of side A; she turns the tape over by feel and presses it on again.

Then Kevin goes around to the passenger side, opens the glovebox himself, takes out a little white bottle with a sponge tip, shuts the glovebox again, and walks the bottle back to the hatch and holds it out to Lena. Kevin says nothing. She takes it.

Jack is in the back on one knee, working the duffel in under the way-back bench where duffels go. Over his head the hatch light is on, and the raised glass is getting letters. They come a stroke at a time, white, on the outside, so that from underneath he gets them backward: WHO DAT · 3 DAYS.
He knows the hand. He puts the duffel in.
Lena is at the open hatch now with both hands on the cargo strap across the bags, taking up the slack.

When he backs out, Laney points him with her chin at the last of her luggage, a quilted train case the size of a tackle box still sitting by Delgado’s side door. He goes and gets it. It is heavier than anything a train case has a right to be, and something inside it clinks.

Theo has walked off to the edge of the lot, past the bike cage where the orange gives out, with his phone to his ear. When it lit up in his hand a minute ago, the screen said *Mom*. Coming back past him with the train case, Jack finds him half turned away with his free hand clamped on top of his head.
“…No. Don’t go in the pool house. Mom. Leave it. I’ll — leave it.”

Theo sees him. He tips the phone away from his mouth. “Sandbags,” he says, and smiles. “They’re saying rain Friday night. The hill behind her house.” The phone goes back to his ear. “Mom. I’m here. I’m listening.”
Jack carries the train case on to the van.

Laney takes it from him at the side door, in the quilted vest and a black-and-gold beanie with a pompom that has no idea what kind of night it is, and stows it under her own seat with her own hands. She has an index card out and is going down it with a Sharpie, ticking as she goes: totes, six; train case; pillows, six; snacks, salty; snacks, sweet; Kevin’s coffee, with DO NOT TOUCH beside it and, in smaller capitals, THEO. She ticks the train case. She keeps hold of the door frame and says one more thing to him, low, and this one doesn’t come through anybody:
“That’s from Julian. For her mama. He’s not coming, if you were wondering. He told her, *It’s your city. I’d be a tourist in it. Go.*”

journal.title: Julian Park-Ellis
journal.text: Julian Park-Ellis. The guitar guy from the Lighthouse stairs. Plays Bastille Thursdays. Wrote a song called “Fresno.” Plays it once a month. All Souls: came to St. Brendan’s to write Nora Calloway’s name in the book. She was his friend. They sang together. He saw us leave in the second chorus. Something new Thursday. A handshake you’d trust with anything. Sunday he came to the nine o’clock with Lena. Didn’t receive. Had the Sanctus by ear by the end. Picked Lena up at twenty to twelve for the vampires, straight from Bastille. Friday he brought her juk in his mother’s thermos and asked her what she’d go to jail for, and listened to all of it. Drove down from Oakland for the nine o’clock; his brother Daniel’s home from the Navy. Two coffees on the wall. Asked me to stay to the end of the new one. Thursday at Bastille: it’s called ‘Magdalena.’ It’s good. The Advent party: plays piano too, by ear. Under contraband mistletoe he kissed her cheek. Kissed her goodbye at his car, for Oakland. Asked me to make sure she eats before her flight. In sixty-one pictures from Lucille’s baptism, at the Broussards’ table between Mémère and Josie. Tess’s caption calls him *le petit violon*. Flew home to Oakland on the fourth. Tuesday morning, on the feed: a picture from their dinner Monday — birthday dinner, two days late; Lena tagged. Songs for Haiti, Friday at Bastille, every dollar to CRS. Theo asked him how many are about her. ‘One.’ At Sully’s Lena introduced him to Skye. ‘The flyers.’ Theo says the new one is about a river. Monday he was at the foot of the Hollis stairs with her bag on his shoulder. He held the door for her, and then for me. He sent a box from Oakland for Mrs. Broussard. He isn’t coming. It’s her city, he told her; he’d be a tourist in it. Laney made sure I heard.

journal.title: Laney Price
journal.text: Laney Price. Pi Lam, as of Thursday: ran back across Seacliff in a pink cowboy hat to Lena first. The night before, on the floor of 217 in a white dress, she asked what happens if they look at her and see. First Catholic Mass: arms crossed like a Baptist, came back from the blessing pink and quiet. Programmed herself into my phone. (Hoodie status: hers.) Pi Lam’s barn party: carried upstairs by her new sisters, glorious and wrecked. Called Lena a mother over the banister. Said sorry at the sign of peace, at her second Mass. Big/Little: Sloane is her big. On the front steps at one in the morning, in a PI LAM LITTLE shirt, with a balloon on her wrist, she told me about Kaylee Whitmore. Fifteen; Kaylee drove; they’d both been drinking and Laney let her. Preston Road. A culvert. A cast for six weeks that everybody signed. A month later, a doctor’s note for flying; she’d never been on a plane. Lena’s the only other one who knows. In the water at Pfeiffer Beach she caught my swan. It’s Theo’s. Her fourth Mass, up a mountain with the monks. Asked Lena how you light a candle, and lit one. Don’t you dare, she said. Halloween: Pope Joan, in a cardboard mitre with gold rickrack. Blessed Del Playa from the widow’s walk until Rafi’s father asked her to come down. Over a bullhorn. Best Couple, with Margot. Went missing with three pledges for most of the extra hour; Kevin found her at Lupe’s with a burrito. She’s not stupid. She’s hungry. Friday at the Situation Room: ‘Who’s that?’ ‘No one.’ Alarm Five: ‘Fireman. You’re dressed.’ Saturday on the laundry table with Theo and a legal pad, discussing finals. Somebody put an orange in her Ugg. She’s crying. The Advent party: black velvet, in mourning for Advent. A Texas thing in the punch; Kevin took her flask. Asleep on the porch swing by a quarter to eleven. The ninth at nine at the Anchor, with an agenda on an index card: pie, no questions. Sunday night she came out of my room with her laptop and went past me without a word. Since Sunday she hasn’t said a word to me. At the Haiti table she met Skye, and gave a hundred dollars to the clipboard. Wednesday night in the lounge she was keeping it short with Theo, for a nod. Then, to me, without turning her head: ‘Night.’ At Sully’s Skye brought her a present. She wore her own bells. She gave Skye advice, and I told her I’ve seen her work. Then she took a shot at Skye, and Skye was handling it, and I didn’t let her. I’ve never yelled at Laney before. The whole bar heard. Tuesday, after the storm, she came back down to the laundry room by herself, with a list: the airport, the status, Sully’s, the jacket, me. She asked what I’m doing. I told her the truth, which I haven’t told anybody. Then I left her standing there. I’m done with that room. Both of them. Friday on the west stairs she and Theo were doing a bit at each other about memory. I said morning. In the lounge she died across the arm of the couch over a picture of tacos. Then she looked at me a long time. Monday night she and Theo were on the lounge floor with two legal pads side by side, and turned them over when I came in. A wedding seating chart, Theo said. Hypothetical. She took ink off my face with her thumb, and went cold again. Thursday night at the van she said she wasn’t Western Union and relayed everything anyway. She packed me a bag: FIREMAN, LARGE. Thirty hours. Behave. She told me Julian isn’t coming, like I’d care, and I told her so.

choices.key: At the van Laney made sure you knew Julian isn’t coming. You asked her why she was telling you.
response: At the open hatch, past the cooler, a pair of hands on a cargo strap stops pulling.

Laney gives his question a long look, as if it’s told her more than he meant it to. “Just keeping the head count, fireman.” Then she looks across the roof of the van at Theo, who is coming back from the edge of the lot with the phone in his pocket, and Theo looks back at her, and whatever goes over the roof goes over it without Jack.

The hands come off the strap. Kevin reaches up for the hatch. “Five a.m.,” he says, to all of them and to Laney in particular. “Not Laney’s five.” The hatch comes down on the loose tail of the strap, and he has to lift it and tuck the tail in and bring it down again.

choices.key: At the van Laney made sure you knew Julian isn’t coming. You told her to put it in the newsletter.
response: Laney doesn’t blink. “Just keeping the head count, fireman.” Her eyes go over the roof of the van to Theo, coming back from the edge of the lot with his phone put away, and Theo meets them, and that is all of it Jack is going to get.
At the hatch a pair of hands has stopped on a cargo strap. They stay stopped a while and then let go.
Kevin brings the hatch down. It shuts on the box from Oakland, riding on the cooler with its twine and its careful capitals. “Five a.m.,” Kevin says. “Not Laney’s five.”

choices.key: At the van Laney made sure you knew Julian isn’t coming. You told her you don’t care.
response: At the open hatch the hands on the cargo strap stop.

Laney looks at him exactly as long as it takes her to be sure of something. “Just keeping the head count, fireman.” Then her eyes go across the roof of the van to Theo. Theo, phone gone, has his hands in his blazer pockets and looks back.
Kevin brings the hatch down, and when it latches the back glass is facing all of them, the right way round: WHO DAT · 3 DAYS. “Five a.m.,” Kevin says. “Not Laney’s five.”

s07b.slug: THURSDAY · 9:10 PM · THE ANACAPA LOT, THE FAR END
body: At the other end of the lot the Odyssey’s dome light goes off, and the van is a dark shape with a rosary in it.

Jack is down by the bike cage where the eucalyptus starts, the orange at his back and the dark going on down toward Del Playa in front of him. The tin is in the left pocket of the Carhartt. The Marlboros are in the right, and his right hand is in there with them, and has been since the hatch came down.

It went fine. A van packed, a seat assigned, a pie on a lap, and not a word to her or from her in an hour, in front of everybody, which is how he wanted it, and how it went. He wants one anyway, the way he wants to sit down at the end of a Saturday close at the Anchor: in the legs first, then the hands, and last of all in anything that thinks. It’s twelve past nine on the RAZR. Nine-thirty is down the hill.

Down there Del Playa is getting its Thursday going, a bass line through somebody’s wall and a girl laughing on a balcony, and under it the surf at the bottom of the bluff. The wind comes up off the water through the cage with kelp in it.

choices.key: After the van, at the far end of the lot, you smoked one.
response: The lighter takes three tries in the wind off the water. He smokes half of it fast, standing at the cage, and puts it out on the post and drops it in the can. On the way down Del Playa toward the house he chews two pieces of Laney’s gum out of FIREMAN, LARGE, which is the first thing in the bag he’s used, and behind him what’s left of the smoke goes back up the hill in the wind, the wrong way, toward the van.

He takes his hand out of the pocket without the pack in it. He starts down Del Playa toward the house with both fists shoved in the Carhartt, the left one around the tin and the right one around nothing, and walks, past the porch lights and the bikes chained to them, until the hands stop wanting anything.

journal.title: The Reliquary
journal.text: An Altoids tin from a pea-soup restaurant in Buellton. RELIQUARY on the lid. No. 1: the Lighthouse. No. 2: Malibu, before breakfast. No. 3: the harbor — she smoked half of it first. No. 4: a clove, on the Delgado roof, at a wake. By dispensation. Do not ask. No. 5: the Ferrer Tower, in the bells. No. 6: Lucia, a motel porch, under the stars — on the back of the receipt. No. 7: Del Playa, on the widow’s walk, on the back of a HALO OR HORNS card. All Hallows — the occasion. No. 8: the east stairs, before light, the morning after All Souls. She smoked half. On the back of an All Souls card — she wrote All Souls anyway. No. 9: Campus Point, Veterans Day, on the back of the 12:10 worship aid. No. 10: the Walgreens on Mission Street, St. Nicholas Eve, half past one in the morning, out of my own pocket. ‘For the saint.’ Into her cardigan. She’ll file it. No. 11: the Point, the last night. She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Thursday night at the far end of the Anacapa lot, after the van: eleven.

response: He opens it under the last lamp. Eleven. He knows it’s eleven. He counts them anyway, with one finger, down the row, and the lid shuts on its little click, and the tin is back in the left pocket before he starts down Del Playa toward the house.

She took it before I could light it. ‘Not here.’ She gave me the tin to keep over Christmas. Count them. Christmas Eve, in Dad’s garage after the levee, I counted: eleven. Thursday night at the far end of the Anacapa lot, after the van: eleven.

response: He opens it under the last lamp and counts them again, with one finger, down the row. Eleven. The lid shuts on its little click, and the tin is back in the left pocket before he starts down Del Playa toward the house.
